questions.q: What is the normal resting coronary blood flow in an adult human, and approximately what percentage of total cardiac output does it represent?
options: 225 to 250 mL/min (about 4% to 5% of cardiac output)
1,200 mL/min (about 20% to 25% of cardiac output)
750 mL/min (about 15% of cardiac output)
50 mL/min (about 1% of cardiac output)
questions.explain: At rest, the coronary arteries receive roughly 225 to 250 mL/min (70 to 80 mL/100 g/min), accounting for 4% to 5% of total cardiac output, and can increase 4- to 5-fold during strenuous exercise.

open.q: State the normal resting coronary blood flow in mL/min and the approximate percentage of resting cardiac output it represents.
accept: 225 to 250 mL/min (4% to 5% of cardiac output)
250 mL/min, 5% of cardiac output

questions.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the majority of blood flow through the left coronary artery into the left ventricular myocardium occur?
options: Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
Ventricular diastole
Rapid ventricular ejection
Reduced ventricular ejection
questions.explain: During left ventricular systole, forceful myocardial contraction compresses intramyocardial subendocardial vessels (extravascular compression), markedly throttling left coronary inflow until diastole relaxes the muscle.

open.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does most left ventricular coronary perfusion occur, and why?
accept: Diastole, because systolic myocardial contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels
Ventricular diastole due to relief of extravascular compression

questions.q: Why is the subendocardial layer of the left ventricle the most vulnerable region to myocardial ischemia during tachycardia or hypotension?
options: It lacks β-adrenergic receptors and cannot respond to sympathetic stimulation.
It receives its entire blood supply from the right coronary artery.
Systolic compression limits flow, so perfusion depends on diastole, which shortens during tachycardia.
Its oxygen extraction is low, so reduced coronary flow causes little ischaemia.
questions.explain: Intramyocardial tissue pressure is highest near the endocardium (equaling intraventricular pressure during systole), making subendocardial vessels wholly dependent on diastolic filling time and aortic diastolic pressure.

open.q: Why is the subendocardium of the left ventricle more susceptible to ischemic injury than the subepicardium?
accept: Highest systolic extravascular compression and sole reliance on diastolic perfusion
Greater systolic tissue compression and lower diastolic perfusion gradient

questions.q: Because resting myocardial oxygen extraction is already near maximum (~65% to 75%), how does the myocardium meet increased oxygen demand during exercise?
options: By increasing oxygen extraction from 70% to 99%
By switching exclusively to anaerobic glycolysis
By lowering heart rate via vagal stimulation
By proportional metabolic coronary vasodilation to increase coronary blood flow
questions.explain: Venous blood in the coronary sinus already has the lowest PO2 (~20 mmHg) in the body; therefore, increased myocardial O2 consumption (MVO2) must be matched almost linearly by local metabolic vasodilation (driven primarily by adenosine, NO, and K+ ATP channels).

open.q: Why must increases in myocardial oxygen demand be met primarily by increasing coronary blood flow rather than increasing oxygen extraction?
accept: Resting myocardial oxygen extraction is already near maximal (65-75%)
Coronary venous blood is already maximally desaturated at rest

questions.q: Which local metabolic vasodilator is considered the single most important physiological mediator matching coronary blood flow to myocardial metabolic demand?
options: Adenosine
Endothelin-1
Angiotensin II
Thromboxane A2
questions.explain: When myocardial ATP breakdown exceeds synthesis during hypoxia or high workload, AMP is dephosphorylated by 5'-nucleotidase into adenosine, which diffuses out of myocytes and potently dilates coronary arterioles via A2A receptors.

open.q: Name the principal local metabolic vasodilator produced from ATP breakdown in cardiac myocytes that couples coronary blood flow to myocardial workload.
accept: Adenosine

questions.q: During sympathetic nervous system activation, direct stimulation of vascular alpha-1 receptors constricts coronary vessels, yet net coronary blood flow increases substantially. What explains this apparent paradox?
options: Sympathetic nerves release acetylcholine onto coronary arterioles
Beta-1-mediated increases in heart rate and contractility boost myocardial metabolism and adenosine/NO release, overriding direct alpha-1 vasoconstriction
Alpha-1 receptors are absent from all human coronary arteries
Coronary veins constrict to push blood backward into capillaries
questions.explain: Metabolic autoregulation dominates neural vasoconstriction in the coronary bed: sympathetic chronotropy and inotropy raise MVO2, generating vasodilator metabolites that dilate resistance arterioles.

open.q: Why does sympathetic stimulation produce net coronary vasodilation despite the presence of alpha-1 vasoconstrictor receptors on coronary vessels?
accept: Increased myocardial metabolism from beta-1 stimulation generates vasodilators (like adenosine) that override alpha-1 constriction
Secondary metabolic vasodilation outweighs direct sympathetic alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction

questions.q: Into which cardiac chamber does the coronary sinus empty most of the venous blood draining the left ventricular myocardium?
options: Left atrium
Left ventricle
Right atrium
Pulmonary trunk
questions.explain: Roughly 75% to 80% of total coronary venous blood drains via the great, middle, and small cardiac veins into the coronary sinus, which opens into the posterior wall of the right atrium between the IVC orifice and tricuspid valve; small Thebesian veins drain directly into all four chambers.

open.q: Into which heart chamber does the coronary sinus empty?
accept: Right atrium

questions.q: What is the normal resting cerebral blood flow (CBF) in an adult human, and over what range of mean arterial pressure (MAP) is it tightly autoregulated?
options: 250 mL/min; autoregulated between 40 and 80 mmHg
1,500 mL/min; autoregulated between 100 and 220 mmHg
300 mL/min; not autoregulated
750 mL/min (~50-55 mL/100 g/min, ~15% of CO); autoregulated between MAP of 60 and 150 mmHg
questions.explain: The brain receives ~750 mL/min (~15% of cardiac output) and maintains constant perfusion via myogenic and metabolic autoregulation across a MAP range of roughly 60 to 150 mmHg (shifted rightward in chronic hypertension).

open.q: State the normal resting cerebral blood flow in mL/min and the mean arterial pressure range over which cerebral autoregulation maintains constant blood flow.
accept: 750 mL/min; MAP 60 to 150 mmHg

questions.q: Which blood gas or chemical factor is the single most potent regulator of cerebral arteriolar diameter and cerebral blood flow?
options: Arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) via interstitial H+ ion concentration
Arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) between 70 and 100 mmHg
Plasma potassium concentration
Circulating epinephrine levels
questions.explain: CO2 freely crosses the blood-brain barrier and hydrates to H2CO3 -> H+ + HCO3-; extracellular H+ potently relaxes cerebral vascular smooth muscle, doubling CBF when PaCO2 rises from 40 to 80 mmHg and halving CBF during hyperventilation hypocapnia.

open.q: What is the most potent physiological regulator of cerebral blood flow, and through which ion does it directly relax cerebral arterioles?
accept: Arterial PCO2 acting via interstitial hydrogen ions (H+)
PaCO2 and CSF/extracellular H+ concentration

questions.q: Why does acute voluntary hyperventilation frequently cause lightheadedness, dizziness, and paresthesias?
options: Hyperventilation raises arterial PO2 to toxic levels that block ATP synthesis
Hyperventilation blows off CO2 (hypocapnia), raising cerebral interstitial pH and causing marked cerebral vasoconstriction that reduces cerebral blood flow
Hyperventilation stimulates massive parasympathetic vasodilation in the brain
Hyperventilation causes sudden systemic arterial hypertension
questions.explain: Lowering PaCO2 from 40 to ~20 mmHg reduces interstitial H+ in the brain, constricting cerebral arterioles and cutting cerebral blood flow by up to 40-50%, while respiratory alkalosis also increases Ca2+ binding to albumin (causing paresthesias).

open.q: Explain the cerebrovascular mechanism by which hyperventilation causes dizziness and lightheadedness.
accept: Hypocapnia lowers cerebral H+ concentration, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and decreased cerebral blood flow
Low arterial PCO2 constricts cerebral arterioles and reduces brain perfusion

questions.q: According to the Monro-Kellie doctrine, what happens inside the rigid adult cranium when an expanding intracranial mass or hemorrhage increases intracranial pressure (ICP)?
options: The adult cranial vault expands to accommodate additional intracranial volume
Cerebral blood flow rises in direct proportion to intracranial pressure
CSF and venous blood are displaced initially; once compensation is exhausted, ICP rises steeply and lowers cerebral perfusion pressure
Arterial pressure immediately falls to equal intracranial pressure
questions.explain: The Monro-Kellie hypothesis states that the sum of brain parenchyma, CSF, and intracranial blood volumes is constant inside the rigid skull; once CSF and venous reserve are exhausted, ICP spikes and compromises CPP (MAP - ICP).

open.q: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine and write the formula for cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in terms of MAP and ICP.
accept: Total intracranial volume (brain + CSF + blood) is constant in a rigid skull; CPP = MAP - ICP
Fixed cranial volume; CPP = Mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure

questions.q: Which anatomical structures form the cellular basis of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)?
options: Fenestrated capillaries with podocyte foot processes form the main cerebral barrier.
Sinusoidal endothelial gaps and Kupffer cells restrict movement into brain tissue.
Stratified squamous epithelium and a basement membrane prevent entry of plasma proteins.
Non-fenestrated endothelial cells with tight junctions, basement membrane, pericytes, and astrocyte end-feet form the BBB.
questions.explain: Continuous tight junctions between cerebral capillary endothelial cells prevent paracellular diffusion of polar solutes, proteins, and neurotransmitters, while astrocyte perivascular end-feet induce and maintain barrier properties.

open.q: Name the key structural components that form the blood-brain barrier.
accept: Tight junctions between non-fenestrated capillary endothelial cells, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes
Endothelial tight junctions and astrocytic end-feet

questions.q: Which midline brain regions are circumventricular organs that lack a blood-brain barrier so they can sample blood-borne hormones and osmolarity directly?
options: Area postrema, subfornical organ, OVLT, and median eminence are key circumventricular organs.
Precentral cortex, Broca area, and primary motor cortex sample circulating hormones directly.
Hippocampus, dentate gyrus, and amygdala lack a BBB to monitor plasma osmolarity.
Substantia nigra, red nucleus, and caudate nucleus are circumventricular structures.
questions.explain: Circumventricular organs have fenestrated capillaries lacking tight junctions: OVLT and subfornical organ sense osmolarity and angiotensin II, area postrema detects emetic toxins, and median eminence/neurohypophysis release hypothalamic hormones.

open.q: Name two circumventricular organs of the brain that lack a blood-brain barrier.
accept: Area postrema and OVLT
Subfornical organ and median eminence
Area postrema and subfornical organ

questions.q: How do normal resting mean pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance compare with systemic arterial pressure and systemic vascular resistance?
options: Pulmonary pressure and resistance are roughly equal to systemic values
Mean pulmonary artery pressure (~15 mmHg; systolic/diastolic ~25/8 mmHg) and pulmonary vascular resistance are roughly one-sixth to one-tenth of systemic values
Mean pulmonary artery pressure is ~95 mmHg, six times higher than systemic
Pulmonary vascular resistance is ten times greater than systemic resistance
questions.explain: The pulmonary circuit is a low-pressure, low-resistance, high-compliance bed (MAP ~15 mmHg vs ~93 mmHg systemic) carrying the entire cardiac output (~5 L/min) across thin alveolar capillaries without causing interstitial pulmonary edema.

open.q: State the normal systolic, diastolic, and mean pulmonary arterial pressures in a healthy adult.
accept: Systolic 25 mmHg, diastolic 8 mmHg, mean 15 mmHg
25/8 mmHg with mean ~15 mmHg

questions.q: How does alveolar hypoxia affect pulmonary arterioles, and what is the physiological purpose of this response?
options: Alveolar hypoxia dilates pulmonary arterioles to increase flow to poorly ventilated units
Alveolar hypoxia has no effect on pulmonary vascular tone
Alveolar hypoxia constricts local pulmonary arterioles, diverting blood toward better-ventilated alveoli
Alveolar hypoxia opens pulmonary arteriovenous shunts
questions.explain: Unique among vascular beds (which dilate in hypoxia), pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar PO2 falls below ~70 mmHg (by inhibiting voltage-gated K+ channels and depolarizing smooth muscle), optimizing V/Q matching; generalized hypoxia (high altitude, COPD) causes pulmonary hypertension.

open.q: Contrast the vascular response to local hypoxia in the pulmonary circulation versus the systemic circulation, and state the physiological benefit of the pulmonary response.
accept: Pulmonary vessels constrict in hypoxia whereas systemic vessels dilate; this shunts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli to maintain V/Q matching
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction redirects blood to better-ventilated lung regions

questions.q: Why does pulmonary vascular resistance decrease (rather than increase) when cardiac output rises 4-fold during heavy exercise?
options: Sympathetic nerves release nitric oxide throughout the lung parenchyma
Alveolar pressure drops to -50 mmHg during exercise
Pulmonary veins actively pump blood into the left atrium
Recruitment of previously closed apical capillaries and distension of already open capillaries expand total cross-sectional area
questions.explain: Higher pulmonary driving pressure opens underperfused apical capillaries (recruitment) and widens compliant capillaries (distension), lowering pulmonary vascular resistance so pulmonary arterial pressure rises only modestly during exercise.

open.q: Name the two passive mechanical mechanisms that lower pulmonary vascular resistance when cardiac output increases during exercise.
accept: Recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries
Capillary recruitment and capillary distension

questions.q: How do changes in lung volume affect extra-alveolar versus alveolar pulmonary blood vessels during deep inspiration?
options: Inspiration stretches extra-alveolar vessels but compresses alveolar capillaries; total resistance is lowest near FRC.
Both vessel groups dilate maximally at TLC, making pulmonary resistance lowest at full inspiration.
Both vessel groups collapse at residual volume, producing the lowest pulmonary resistance.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is independent of lung volume because vessel calibre is fixed.
questions.explain: During deep inflation, expanding alveoli compress alveolar wall capillaries, while outward parenchymal tethering pulls open larger extra-alveolar vessels; at very low volumes, extra-alveolar vessels narrow, so total PVR forms a U-shaped curve with its minimum at FRC.

open.q: At which lung volume is total pulmonary vascular resistance at its minimum, and why?
accept: Functional residual capacity (FRC), because alveolar capillaries are not over-compressed and extra-alveolar vessels are not collapsed
FRC (balances alveolar capillary compression at high volumes against extra-alveolar vessel narrowing at low volumes)

questions.q: What percentage of resting cardiac output is received by the two kidneys combined (~1,100 to 1,200 mL/min), and why is this flow rate so high?
options: 5%; solely to meet renal metabolic oxygen consumption
20% to 25%; primarily to supply high plasma volume for glomerular filtration rather than metabolic oxygen demand
50%; to warm blood returning from the lower extremities
2%; because renal arterioles are tonically constricted
questions.explain: Renal blood flow (~1.1-1.2 L/min, ~20-25% of CO) far exceeds the kidneys' modest metabolic O2 requirement (renal arteriovenous O2 difference is only ~1.5 mL/dL), serving to generate a glomerular filtration rate of ~125 mL/min.

open.q: State the normal resting renal blood flow in mL/min (and percentage of cardiac output) and explain its primary physiological purpose.
accept: 1,100 to 1,200 mL/min (20-25% of CO) to provide sufficient plasma flow for glomerular filtration
~1.2 L/min (~22% of CO) to maintain high glomerular filtration rate

questions.q: Which unique anatomical arrangement of two capillary beds connected in series exists in the renal cortex?
options: Hepatic sinusoids drain directly into central veins before blood reaches the portal vein.
Alveolar capillaries drain into bronchial veins before returning to the left atrium.
Glomerular capillaries drain through the efferent arteriole into peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
Coronary capillaries drain directly into the pulmonary veins through Thebesian channels.
questions.explain: The efferent arteriole separates the high-pressure glomerular capillary tuft (~55-60 mmHg, specialized for filtration) from the low-pressure peritubular capillary network (~13-15 mmHg, specialized for tubular fluid reabsorption).

open.q: Name the two capillary beds arranged in series in the renal cortex and the blood vessel that connects them.
accept: Glomerular capillaries and peritubular capillaries connected by the efferent arteriole
Glomerulus -> efferent arteriole -> peritubular capillaries

questions.q: Which two intrinsic mechanisms autoregulate renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) across a mean arterial pressure range of 80 to 180 mmHg?
options: Carotid sinus baroreflex and Bainbridge reflex
Hypoxic vasoconstriction and pulmonary capillary recruitment
Hepatic arterial buffer response and portal venous compliance
Myogenic stretch response of afferent arterioles and tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) mediated by the macula densa
questions.explain: When renal arterial pressure rises, afferent arterioles constrict myogenically while increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa releases ATP/adenosine to constrict the afferent arteriole (TGF), keeping RBF and GFR nearly constant.

open.q: Name the two intrinsic autoregulatory mechanisms that stabilize renal blood flow and GFR between MAP 80 and 180 mmHg.
accept: Myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback
Afferent arteriolar myogenic response and macula densa tubuloglomerular feedback

questions.q: How is blood flow distributed between the renal cortex and the renal medulla, and why is medullary blood flow kept sluggish?
options: Most renal blood flow supplies cortex; slower vasa recta flow helps preserve the medullary osmotic gradient.
Most renal blood flow supplies medulla, while cortical flow is limited to protect glomeruli.
Cortex and medulla receive equal flow, maintaining identical oxygen tension throughout the kidney.
The medulla is avascular and receives oxygen only by diffusion from the cortex.
questions.explain: Slow blood flow through the hairpin-loop vasa recta (~5-10% of RBF) acts as a countercurrent exchanger that supplies oxygen to medullary tubules without washing away the hyperosmolar NaCl and urea gradient needed to concentrate urine.

open.q: What percentage of total renal blood flow supplies the renal cortex versus the renal medulla, and why must medullary blood flow remain low?
accept: 90-95% to cortex and 5-10% to medulla; low medullary flow preserves the medullary osmotic gradient
~90% cortical, ~10% medullary so vasa recta do not wash out medullary hyperosmolarity

questions.q: What percentage of total hepatic blood flow (~1,500 mL/min) is supplied by the hepatic portal vein versus the hepatic artery, and how do their oxygen contributions compare?
options: The portal vein supplies one quarter of flow and most hepatic oxygen
Portal vein supplies about 75% of hepatic flow and hepatic artery 25%; each contributes roughly half of hepatic oxygen
Portal and hepatic arterial flow are equal, and the hepatic artery supplies all oxygen
The portal vein supplies almost all hepatic flow but contributes no oxygen
questions.explain: The liver receives ~1,500 mL/min (~25-30% of CO): ~1,100 mL/min (75%) via the portal vein (PO2 ~50-60 mmHg) and ~400 mL/min (25%) via the hepatic artery (PO2 ~95 mmHg); because portal flow is three times larger, both vessels deliver ~50% of hepatic O2.

open.q: Compare the blood flow contributions and oxygen delivery contributions of the portal vein and hepatic artery to the liver.
accept: Portal vein supplies ~75% of blood flow and ~50% of O2; hepatic artery supplies ~25% of blood flow and ~50% of O2
75% portal venous flow / 25% hepatic arterial flow; roughly 50% oxygen from each

questions.q: What is the hepatic arterial buffer response (HABR)?
options: Reflex constriction of the hepatic artery whenever portal venous flow drops
Storage of excess red blood cells inside hepatic sinusoids during exercise
Compensatory dilation of the hepatic artery when portal venous blood flow decreases (and vice versa), mediated by local adenosine washout
Conversion of portal venous blood directly into bile salts
questions.explain: Adenosine is continuously secreted into the space of Mall around hepatic arterioles and portal venules; when portal flow falls, less adenosine is washed away, so local adenosine accumulates and dilates the hepatic artery to stabilize total liver perfusion.

open.q: Describe the hepatic arterial buffer response and name the local vasodilator mediator that regulates it.
accept: Compensatory hepatic arterial dilation when portal venous flow decreases, mediated by reduced washout of adenosine
Inverse adjustment of hepatic arterial flow to portal venous flow via adenosine

questions.q: What is postprandial hyperemia in the gastrointestinal tract, and which factors mediate it?
options: Digestion reduces mesenteric flow through sympathetic vasoconstriction and lowers mucosal metabolism.
Dietary fibre constricts villous capillaries and diverts blood to skeletal muscle.
Portal flow stops temporarily while nutrients are absorbed from the small intestine.
GI blood flow rises after meals through local metabolites, hormones, and nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation.
questions.explain: Digestive secretions, motility, and active nutrient transport raise mucosal metabolic demand, releasing adenosine, K+, CO2, nitric oxide, and gut peptides (CCK, neurotensin, VIP) that dilate splanchnic arterioles.

open.q: Define postprandial splanchnic hyperemia and name three mediators responsible for it.
accept: Increased GI blood flow after a meal mediated by CCK, gastrin, secretin, adenosine, and nitric oxide
Post-meal mesenteric vasodilation driven by gut hormones and local metabolic vasodilators

questions.q: Why does the splanchnic vascular bed serve as an important blood reservoir during acute hemorrhage or vigorous exercise?
options: Splanchnic veins and hepatic sinusoids form a compliant blood reservoir that can mobilise blood during sympathetic activation
The human spleen normally stores several litres of packed red cells
Splanchnic arteries dilate maximally during haemorrhagic shock
Portal venous pressure rises to arterial levels during exercise
questions.explain: Unlike dogs and horses (which have large contractile spleens), the human spleen stores only ~50-100 mL of blood; instead, the liver and splanchnic venous capacitance vessels act as the primary human blood reservoir.

open.q: How does the splanchnic circulation act as a major blood volume reservoir during acute hemorrhage or strenuous exercise in humans?
accept: Sympathetic alpha-1 stimulation constricts compliant splanchnic veins and hepatic sinusoids, mobilizing stored blood into the central venous circulation
Alpha-adrenergic venoconstriction of splanchnic vessels autotransfuses blood back to the heart

questions.q: What is the primary physiological function of the cutaneous circulation in humans, and across what wide range can skin blood flow vary?
options: Meeting high basal skin oxygen demand; varies narrowly between 200 and 250 mL/min
Thermoregulation (heat conservation vs heat dissipation); varies from as low as 20-30 mL/min in extreme cold to 2,000-3,000 mL/min in severe heat stress
Filtering metabolic nitrogenous wastes; varies between 1,000 and 1,200 mL/min
Oxygenating systemic venous blood; fixed at 500 mL/min
questions.explain: Nutritional blood flow required by skin cells is tiny (~20-30 mL/min), so skin perfusion is governed chiefly by hypothalamic thermoregulatory signals, expanding over 100-fold in extreme heat to radiate and conduct heat.

open.q: What is the primary physiological role of cutaneous blood flow, and roughly how wide is its flow range from extreme cold to extreme heat?
accept: Thermoregulation; ranges from ~20-30 mL/min in severe cold to 2,000-3,000 mL/min in extreme heat
Body temperature regulation; ~25 mL/min up to 3 L/min

questions.q: Which specialized vascular structures in glabrous (non-hairy) skin of the palms, soles, fingertips, ears, and nose bypass nutritional capillaries to allow rapid heat loss?
options: Vasa recta
Coronary sinusoids
Arteriovenous anastomoses (AV shunts)
Fenestrated glomerular tufts
questions.explain: Thick-walled, muscular arteriovenous anastomoses connect small arteries directly to venous plexuses in acral skin; they lack metabolic control and are controlled purely by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves (opening when sympathetic tone is withdrawn).

open.q: Name the specialized direct vascular shunts in the skin of the hands, feet, ears, and nose that rapidly transfer heat to the venous plexus.
accept: Arteriovenous anastomoses
AV anastomoses
AV shunts

questions.q: How do sympathetic sudomotor (cholinergic) fibers contribute to active cutaneous vasodilation in non-acral hairy skin during heat stress?
options: Sympathetic fibres release noradrenaline onto α1 receptors to constrict cutaneous arterioles.
Keratinocyte endothelin release is the main mechanism of sweat-associated vasodilation.
Sudomotor activity suppresses sweat secretion and reduces skin blood flow during heat stress.
Cholinergic fibres release acetylcholine and cotransmitters that support sweating and active vasodilation.
questions.explain: In non-acral skin, warming first withdraws sympathetic noradrenergic vasoconstrictor tone, and further core warming activates sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor nerves that stimulate sweating and release vasodilator co-transmitters (VIP, NO, prostaglandins).

open.q: How does active cutaneous vasodilation occur in hairy skin during whole-body heat stress?
accept: Sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor nerves release acetylcholine and vasodilator co-transmitters (VIP/NO) alongside sweat gland activation
Sympathetic cholinergic nerves stimulate sweating and release vasodilators such as VIP and nitric oxide

questions.q: What are the three sequential components of the Lewis triple response observed when the skin is firmly stroked with a blunt pointed instrument?
options: The response comprises a local red reaction, an axon-reflex flare, and a wheal from increased permeability.
The response comprises blanching, cyanosis, and necrosis from sustained vasoconstriction.
The response comprises sweating, piloerection, and shivering from sympathetic activation.
The response comprises petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses from capillary rupture.
questions.explain: Firm mechanical trauma causes: (1) Red line at the stroke site (direct histamine/NO capillary dilation), (2) Surrounding red flare (antidromic C-fiber axon reflex releasing substance P and CGRP), and (3) Raised wheal (histamine-mediated venular exudation).

open.q: List the three components of Lewis's triple response in skin and identify which component is mediated by a local nociceptive axon reflex.
accept: Red reaction, flare (axon reflex), and wheal
Red line, flare (mediated by C-fiber axon reflex), and wheal

questions.q: What is the hunting reaction of Lewis (cold-induced vasodilation) during prolonged immersion of the fingers in ice water?
options: Cold causes sustained vasodilation from the start, preventing any reduction in digital blood flow.
Initial vasoconstriction is followed by intermittent vasodilation that temporarily restores digital blood flow.
Cold triggers continuous sweating and loss of heat from the fingers.
Cold exposure causes systemic arterial pressure to fall to zero during immersion.
questions.explain: Severe cold initially constricts cutaneous vessels, but below ~10-15 C smooth muscle loses responsiveness to norepinephrine and cold paralyzes sympathetic nerve conduction, causing transient vasodilation that rewarms the finger before constriction cycles again.

open.q: Describe Lewis's hunting reaction (cold-induced vasodilation) in extremities exposed to severe cold.
accept: Initial cold-induced vasoconstriction followed by periodic bursts of vasodilation to protect tissues from freezing
Cyclic vasodilation interrupting prolonged cold vasoconstriction

questions.q: How is skeletal muscle blood flow regulated at rest versus during intense rhythmic contraction?
options: Local metabolic vasodilation dominates at rest, while alpha-1 constriction dominates during exercise
Muscle blood flow remains fixed at rest and during maximal exercise
Sympathetic tone limits resting flow; local metabolites override it during exercise and markedly increase perfusion
Vagal parasympathetic fibres directly dilate all skeletal muscle arterioles
questions.explain: At rest, only ~20-25% of skeletal muscle capillaries are open due to tonic sympathetic alpha-1 constriction; during exercise, local metabolic vasodilators produce functional sympatholysis, opening dormant capillaries and raising muscle blood flow up to 20-fold.

open.q: Compare the dominant control of skeletal muscle blood flow at rest versus during strenuous exercise.
accept: Sympathetic alpha-1 vasoconstrictor tone dominates at rest; local metabolic vasodilators dominate during exercise
Neural vasoconstriction at rest vs local metabolic vasodilation during exercise

questions.q: Why does sustained isometric (static) muscle contraction (such as heavy weightlifting) cause a sharp rise in mean arterial pressure while temporarily impeding blood flow through the contracting muscle?
options: Static contraction suppresses sympathetic outflow and causes widespread vasodilation.
Static contraction opens venous valves in reverse and increases venous return.
Static contraction produces reflex bradycardia and reduces systemic vascular resistance.
Intramuscular pressure compresses vessels while the exercise pressor reflex raises sympathetic drive and arterial pressure.
questions.explain: Above ~20-30% of maximal voluntary contraction, sustained intramuscular pressure squeezes blood vessels shut (stopping rhythmic muscle-pump assistance), while metabolite buildup excites group III/IV muscle afferents (exercise pressor reflex) to boost sympathetic BP.

open.q: Why does sustained static (isometric) exercise raise blood pressure more sharply than rhythmic dynamic exercise while reducing local blood flow during the contraction?
accept: Sustained intramuscular tension mechanically compresses blood vessels and activates the metaboreceptor exercise pressor reflex
Mechanical vessel compression impedes flow and stimulates sympathetic pressor reflexes

questions.q: Which fetal vascular shunt carries oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein directly into the inferior vena cava, largely bypassing the fetal hepatic sinusoids?
options: Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
Ligamentum teres
questions.explain: The umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood (PO2 ~30-35 mmHg, ~80% saturated) from the placenta; roughly half bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus directly into the IVC.

open.q: Name the fetal vascular shunt that routes oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver.
accept: Ductus venosus

questions.q: Which two fetal shunts divert most right-sided cardiac output away from the high-resistance, fluid-filled fetal lungs into the systemic circulation?
options: The ductus venosus and umbilical arteries divert blood away from the fetal lungs.
The foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the high-resistance fetal pulmonary circulation.
The coronary sinus and azygos vein divert right ventricular output into systemic arteries.
The superior vena cava and portal vein connect the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta.
questions.explain: Because fetal alveoli are unexpanded and hypoxic, pulmonary vascular resistance is very high; right atrial blood streams across the foramen ovale to the left atrium (perfusing heart and brain), while right ventricular blood passes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta.

open.q: Name the two fetal circulatory shunts that allow blood to bypass the unexpanded fetal lungs.
accept: Foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus
Ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale

questions.q: What triggers the functional closure of the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus immediately after birth?
options: Reduced oxygen and increased prostaglandin E2 close the ductus arteriosus
Clamping the superior vena cava raises right atrial pressure and closes the foramen ovale
Lung expansion raises left atrial pressure; increased oxygen and reduced PGE2 constrict the ductus arteriosus
Placental blood flow increases and systemic pressure falls after the first breath
questions.explain: The first breath expands the lungs, slashing pulmonary vascular resistance and increasing pulmonary venous return so left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum; simultaneously, high arterial PO2 and loss of placental PGE2 constrict ductus arteriosus smooth muscle.

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanisms that close both the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus at birth.
accept: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance and raises left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure to close the foramen ovale; rising arterial PO2 and falling PGE2 constrict the ductus arteriosus
Reversal of interatrial pressure gradient closes foramen ovale; increased PO2 and decreased prostaglandins close ductus arteriosus

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry deoxygenated fetal blood back to the placenta, and from which maternal/fetal vessels do they arise?
options: Single umbilical vein arising from the fetal portal vein
Two umbilical veins arising from the fetal pulmonary veins
Single umbilical artery arising from the fetal ascending aorta
Two umbilical arteries arising from the fetal internal iliac arteries
questions.explain: The umbilical cord normally contains two umbilical arteries (branches of the fetal internal iliac arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (returning oxygenated blood to the fetus).

open.q: How many umbilical arteries and umbilical veins are present in a normal human umbilical cord, and which carries oxygenated blood?
accept: Two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated) and one umbilical vein (oxygenated)
2 arteries and 1 vein; the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood

questions.q: A 62-year-old man experiences retrosternal chest tightness consistently after walking briskly up two flights of stairs, relieved within 3 minutes of rest or sublingual nitroglycerin. Coronary angiography reveals a 75% fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of the left anterior descending artery. Which physiological principle explains why he has no chest pain at rest?
options: Coronary autoregulatory vasodilation distal to the stenosis preserves resting blood flow until coronary flow reserve is exhausted during exercise
Collateral vessels completely bypass the stenosis only during sleep
Nitroglycerin selectively constricts the left anterior descending artery
Myocardial oxygen demand drops during stair climbing
questions.explain: Downstream resistance arterioles dilate progressively to compensate for upstream epicardial stenosis, maintaining normal resting flow up to ~70% diameter narrowing; once maximal dilation (coronary flow reserve) is exhausted during exertion, demand outstrips supply, causing stable angina.

open.q: Why does a 70% to 75% fixed coronary artery stenosis typically produce angina during exertion while remaining asymptomatic at rest?
accept: Downstream autoregulatory vasodilation maintains resting flow, but coronary flow reserve is exhausted when exercise raises myocardial oxygen demand
Exhaustion of coronary flow reserve during increased myocardial workload

questions.q: A 48-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presents with hematemesis from esophageal varices, caput medusae, splenomegaly, and ascites. Elevated pressure in which vascular system directly drives these clinical signs?
options: Pulmonary venous circulation
Hepatic portal venous system (portal hypertension)
Coronary sinus circulation
Internal carotid arterial system
questions.explain: Hepatic fibrosis and regenerative nodules compress hepatic sinusoids, raising sinusoidal and portal venous pressure above 10-12 mmHg and forcing blood through portosystemic anastomoses (esophageal, paraumbilical, and hemorrhoidal veins).

open.q: Elevation of pressure in which venous circulation causes esophageal varices, caput medusae, and splenomegaly in liver cirrhosis?
accept: Portal venous circulation
Hepatic portal system
Portal hypertension

questions.q: A 30-year-old man sustains severe head trauma in a motorcycle collision and develops an acute epidural hematoma with rising intracranial pressure. His blood pressure rises to 196/104 mmHg, his heart rate drops to 44 beats/min, and his breathing becomes irregular. What is the physiological explanation for his hypertension and bradycardia?
options: Scalp blood loss causes hypovolaemia and compensatory hyperventilation
Carotid sinus destruction causes isolated hypertension and bradycardia
Raised ICP triggers medullary ischaemia and sympathetic hypertension, followed by baroreflex bradycardia
Excess brain natriuretic peptide directly slows the sinoatrial node
questions.explain: In the Cushing reflex, high ICP threatens cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP), evoking a powerful CNS ischemic sympathetic surge to raise MAP above ICP; the resulting severe hypertension activates carotid/aortic baroreceptors, triggering reflex vagal bradycardia.

open.q: Explain the sequential physiological mechanism producing both hypertension and bradycardia in the Cushing reflex.
accept: Raised ICP causes medullary ischemia and intense sympathetic vasoconstriction (hypertension), which then triggers baroreceptor-mediated vagal bradycardia
CNS ischemic sympathetic surge raises BP, followed by baroreceptor reflex slowing of heart rate

questions.q: A premature neonate born at 29 weeks gestation has a continuous machinery-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area and bounding pulses due to a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Administration of indomethacin successfully closes the ductus by inhibiting which enzyme?
options: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)
HMG-CoA reductase
Cyclooxygenase (COX), thereby blocking vasodilatory prostaglandin E2 synthesis
questions.explain: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) actively keeps the ductus arteriosus patent in utero; NSAIDs like indomethacin or ibuprofen inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) to lower PGE2 and promote smooth muscle constriction and closure.

open.q: By inhibiting which enzyme and lowering which endogenous vasodilator does indomethacin promote closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)?
accept: Cyclooxygenase (COX) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)
COX enzyme, reducing prostaglandin E2
